interactions.summary: The host frames the interview around whether history can still be protected from geopolitical manipulation after the twentieth century and the rhetoric of the 'right side of history.'
Jiang gives a brief courtesy acceptance before the substantive questioning begins.
The host summarizes psychohistory as applying psychoanalysis to geopolitics and asks why entrenched power holders would ever let a wiser predictive understanding of social behavior benefit humanity.

Jiang defines psychohistory as psychoanalysis joined to game theory, models nation-states as persons with memory and motive, argues empathy and historical behavior make prediction possible, and says elite hubris eventually collapses societies so later elites can rebuild on better historical standards.

The host argues that serious history requires a non-narcissistic reading of past human dynamics, then asks how Jiang navigates Western claims to stand on the 'right side of history' when those claims also intimidate dissenters.

Jiang replies that history is usually taught as indoctrination rather than objective inquiry, treats Fukuyama-style end-of-history liberal triumphalism as propaganda, and says neoliberal history-writing serves colonial exploitation, inequality, corruption, and war.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang compresses his whole method into a psychological reading of states as if they were persons whose past behavior can be empathically modeled.
signature_moments.source_phrase: I see nation states as individuals
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the packet's governing move: geopolitics becomes legible by importing person-level memory, motive, and empathy into state analysis.

signature_moments.moment: Elite rule appears here as a tragic cycle in which arrogance destroys the very society it tries to dominate, clearing the way for a replacement order.
signature_moments.source_phrase: because of their hubris, because of their arrogance, they will lead their societies to collapse
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It sets Jiang's cyclical theory of political succession and explains why he answers elite capture with long-duration historical turnover rather than immediate reform.

signature_moments.moment: History is recast from neutral scholarship into an ideological weapon wielded by victors.
signature_moments.source_phrase: history is not an objective study of the human condition. It's really a tool of indoctrination
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the interview's first sharp reversal: the standard archive of history is itself accused of being part of the problem Jiang is trying to solve.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang answers liberal triumphalism by calling neoliberalism not progress but a colonial extraction machine.
signature_moments.source_phrase: Neoliberalism is just a mechanism of colonial exploitation
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It gives the packet its strongest polemical edge and anchors his refusal to treat post-Cold War Western ideology as historically vindicated.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Used here for Jiang's method of combining psychoanalysis with game theory to model the behavior of nation-states and generate predictive geopolitical frameworks.
Used by the host as a dominant recent Western narrative that claims moral and historical inevitability while intimidating dissent.
Invoked as Fukuyama's post-Soviet thesis that consumer liberal democracy had proven itself the best final system; Jiang cites it as propaganda.

chronology_notes.note: The interview opens by situating itself after the twentieth century and after the recent rise of 'right side of history' rhetoric, framing the source as a response to a contemporary ideological climate rather than as a timeless theory talk.

This opening packet establishes Jiang's core sequence before later case studies: define psychohistory, explain elite-cycle collapse, then attack the dominant liberal historical narrative as indoctrination.
